entities.summary:
Heimskringla, written by the Icelandic historian Snorri Sturluson around 1225, is a seminal collection of sagas that chronicles the lives and reigns of the kings of Norway. This text serves as a vital source for understanding the medieval Scandinavian history and Norse mythology, detailing over 30 kings from the legendary figure of Harald Fairhair to the historical King Håkon IV. Sturluson, a prominent figure in Icelandic literature, utilized oral traditions and earlier texts to weave a narrative that not only preserved the history of Norway but also reflected the complex interplay of politics and culture in medieval Europe.

The creation of Heimskringla was influenced by the sociopolitical landscape of 13th-century Norway, which was marked by the consolidation of power under the monarchy and the introduction of Christianity. Through its vivid storytelling, Heimskringla not only narrates historical events but also provides insights into the values, beliefs, and customs of the Viking Age, offering a glimpse into the societal structure and the significance of kinship and honor among the Norse people. The sagas are enriched with detailed genealogies, battles, and the interactions between Norway and other kingdoms, such as Denmark and Sweden, showcasing the regional dynamics of power during this era.

The legacy of Heimskringla extends beyond its immediate historical context, influencing subsequent generations of historians, poets, and playwrights. Its narratives contributed to the development of national identity in Norway, particularly during the Romantic period, when there was a resurgence of interest in Norse heritage. The sagas have been translated into numerous languages, remaining a cornerstone for those studying Viking history and literature. As historian Peter Hallberg noted, 'Heimskringla is not just a history but a mirror reflecting the soul of a nation.'

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Heimskringla (Old Norse: 'The Circle of the World', or 'The Orb of the World') is a collection of sagas of the Norwegian kings (konungasögur) written in Old Norse by the Icelandic scholar and statesman Snorri Sturluson (1179–1241), probably composed c. 1230 CE — the most comprehensive and historically authoritative account of the Norwegian kings from the legendary origins of the Norse royal dynasties to the reign of Magnus Erlingsson (d. 1184), and the primary source for the history of Norway and Scandinavia from the Viking Age to the 12th century. Heimskringla comprises sixteen sagas, beginning with the Ynglinga saga (a mythological account of the origins of the Yngling dynasty, drawing on Snorri's Prose Edda, Scandinavian mythology, and the traditions of the Swedish royal house) and continuing through the historical sagas of the Norwegian kings: Hákon góði, Óláfr Tryggvason, Óláfr Haraldsson (St. Olaf), Magnús góði, Haráldr harðráði, and others, concluding with the saga of Magnus Erlingsson.

Snorri Sturluson is the most important figure in the preservation of Old Norse literary and historical tradition — his Prose Edda (a handbook of Norse mythology and poetic technique, c. 1220) and Heimskringla together constitute the primary sources for our knowledge of Norse mythology, the skaldic poetic tradition, and the history of early medieval Norway. Snorri was himself a major Icelandic political figure — a chieftain, twice lawspeaker of the Althing (Iceland's parliament), and an important player in the complex Norwegian-Icelandic political relations of the 13th century — who was eventually assassinated in 1241 on the orders of the Norwegian King Hákon Hákonarson.
